data.targetWord: The belief that after death a person will rise again in bodily form, as held in Christianity and Islam

examples.en-GB: Christian belief in resurrection is based on the resurrection of Jesus, which gives hope for eternal life.

data.targetWord: In Christianity and Islam, a state or place of eternal happiness and closeness to God after death

examples.en-GB: Christians believe heaven is a state of eternal life in God's presence for those who are saved.

data.targetWord: A state of punishment or separation from God after death; interpreted differently across traditions as permanent punishment, purification, or annihilation

examples.en-GB: Christians hold different views on hell — some see it as eternal separation from God; others as annihilation.

data.targetWord: In Catholic teaching, a state of purification after death before entering heaven, where the soul is prepared for God's presence

examples.en-GB: Purgatory is a Catholic teaching — other Christian traditions do not hold this belief.

data.targetWord: The Islamic term for life after death, including judgement, Jannah (paradise), and Jahannam (hell); one of the Six Articles of Faith

examples.en-GB: Belief in Akhirah shapes Muslim ethics — all actions are recorded and will be judged.

data.targetWord: The Islamic concept of paradise — a beautiful state of peace, joy, and closeness to Allah for those whose good deeds outweigh bad

examples.en-GB: Jannah is described in the Qur'an as a garden of rivers, shade, and perfect peace.

data.targetWord: The Islamic concept of hell — a place of punishment for those who rejected Allah or acted wrongly

examples.en-GB: Some Muslim scholars teach that Jahannam is temporary purification for believers, not eternal for all.

data.targetWord: The Islamic Day of Judgement, when all people are raised from the dead and their deeds are weighed before Allah

examples.en-GB: On Yawm al-Qiyama, each person receives their Book of Deeds and is judged by Allah.

data.targetWord: In Islam, the state or period between death and the Day of Resurrection, in which the soul waits

examples.en-GB: Barzakh is a transitional state — the soul is between death and its final judgement.

data.targetWord: The Hindu belief that a permanent soul (atman) passes through many different bodies across many lifetimes

examples.en-GB: Reincarnation in Hinduism means the atman returns in a new body, shaped by karma.

data.targetWord: In Hinduism, liberation from the cycle of samsara (rebirth); the atman merges with or finds rest in Brahman

examples.en-GB: Moksha is the ultimate goal of Hindu spiritual life — freedom from the cycle of rebirth.

data.targetWord: The Buddhist teaching that a stream of consciousness continues into a new life after death, shaped by karma — distinct from Hindu reincarnation as there is no permanent self

examples.en-GB: Buddhist rebirth is like a candle lighting another candle — there is continuity but no fixed, unchanged entity.

data.targetWord: In Buddhism, liberation from craving and the cycle of rebirth; the extinguishing of suffering — not a paradise but freedom from all that drives samsara

examples.en-GB: Nirvana is the Buddhist ultimate goal — not heaven, but the ending of craving and rebirth.

data.targetWord: The Sikh term for liberation — union with Waheguru (God), achieved through God's grace and following the Gurus' teachings, freeing the soul from the cycle of rebirth

examples.en-GB: Mukti in Sikhism is achieved through God's grace (nadar), not solely through one's own efforts.

data.targetWord: The humanist understanding of how a person 'lives on' — through memories, relationships, and the lasting influence of their life — without personal survival of consciousness

examples.en-GB: For humanists, legacy means that a person continues in the memories and lives of those they have touched.

data.targetWord: Hebrew for 'the World to Come'; a Jewish concept of a future age of peace, restoration, and in some traditions resurrection of the dead

examples.en-GB: Olam Ha-Ba is the traditional Jewish term for the afterlife, though Jewish views on it are varied.

data.targetWord: The Jewish seven-day period of mourning after a death, during which the family gathers at home for prayer and communal support

examples.en-GB: During shiva, friends and family visit the bereaved to offer comfort and share memories.

data.targetWord: The cycle of birth, death, and rebirth found in Hinduism, Buddhism, and Sikhism, from which liberation is the ultimate goal

examples.en-GB: Moksha, nirvana, and mukti are all different terms for liberation from samsara.

data.targetWord: The belief that after death God will assess a person's life and deeds, determining their eternal fate

examples.en-GB: In Islam, judgement happens on Yawm al-Qiyama; in Christianity, God judges each person after death.

data.targetWord: The immaterial, spiritual aspect of a person believed in many traditions to survive death; understood very differently across traditions

examples.en-GB: Hindu and Buddhist traditions have very different views of the soul — the atman is permanent; anatta says there is none.

data.title: Place the stages of the Islamic afterlife in the correct order
items: Death — the soul (ruh) departs the body
Barzakh — the soul waits in a state between death and resurrection
Yawm al-Qiyama — the Day of Judgement; all are raised and deeds weighed
The righteous enter Jannah (paradise); the wrongdoers face Jahannam (hell)

data.title: Arrange the three main afterlife frameworks from most to least centred on personal identity
items: Resurrection — the same person rises again in transformed bodily form
Reincarnation/rebirth — a soul or consciousness continues in a new life
Legacy — no personal survival; living on through memory and influence only

data.title: Arrange the stages of the Hindu soul's journey in the correct order
items: The atman lives within a body during one lifetime
The body dies — the atman leaves the body (cremation releases it)
Karma shapes the quality of the next life — the atman is reborn
Through dharma and devotion, the atman achieves moksha — liberation from samsara

pairs.text: Christianity — the same person rises in transformed bodily form
Islam — all are raised on Yawm al-Qiyama
Hinduism — the atman passes through many bodies
Sikhism — the soul is reborn until union with Waheguru
Buddhism — a stream of consciousness continues without a permanent self
Humanism — the person lives on only in memory and legacy
Moksha — liberation of the atman from samsara
Samsara — the cycle of birth, death, and rebirth
Reincarnation — the atman moves between bodies
Barzakh — the waiting state between death and resurrection
Yawm al-Qiyama — the Day of Judgement
